blocks.text: I kept walking until the hospital was out of sight. My lungs still burned, and the shoes pinched at my toes. I had Lidia’s ID in my pocket. I kept touching it through the cloth like it could tell me what to do next.
I knew the road to her house from visits years earlier, before I was locked away.

I took a bus part of the way, then walked the last stretch because I didn’t want to arrive at the door breathing hard and looking scared. That sounds foolish now. I was scared. I just didn’t want Damian to see it first.

At a little shop near the main road, I asked the woman behind the counter if I could use her phone if I needed to. I didn’t call yet. I wanted to see Sofi, and I told myself that if I called before I knew where she was, I might make things worse. That was the first bad choice I made that night. I know it now.

I reached the house after dark. I remember the front step had a crack through the middle, because I nearly caught my shoe in it. I stood there for a few seconds, listening. A television was on inside. I could hear a woman talking over it.
Damian opened the door. He looked straight at my face and said, “You’re late.”
That was all. No second look, no question. He stepped aside, and I walked in.

His mother was at the table with a stack of folded clothes. His sister sat near the television, scrolling on her phone. Neither one looked surprised to see me. Damian went back to the room where he’d been sitting and kept watching the screen.

I didn’t know the house well enough to pretend I knew where everything was, but I knew Lidia’s hands. I knew the way she’d told me she had to move through that place carefully, trying not to give any of them a reason to get mad. I watched the mother push a basket of laundry toward me with her foot.
His sister glanced up. “And the dishes.”
I looked at the basket. Then at the sink. I could feel my own anger trying to get ahead of me, so I made myself take one breath before I answered.
I told them I had a headache. The words sounded wrong in my mouth. Lidia might have said them softly. I couldn’t make myself do that.

I didn’t answer. I looked past her, toward the short hall. I needed to find Sofi. That was the only thing that mattered, and still I was standing there thinking about laundry, because the room had made that seem like the job I was supposed to do.

Damian didn’t look away from the television. He asked if I’d made dinner. When I said no, he sighed like I’d ruined his evening. His mother gave a little shake of her head. His sister returned to her phone.

I don’t know why I expected some grand sign of what Lidia had been living with. There wasn’t one. It was a basket, a sink, people speaking to her as if she were there to serve them. Ordinary things. That was what made it worse.
His mother said she was in the back room. Damian finally turned his head. “Why?”
I said I wanted to see her. He gave me a look I couldn’t read, or maybe I just didn’t want to. Then he turned back to the television. His mother’s eyes stayed on me as I walked down the hall.
Sofi was on the floor with a few toys. She looked up when I came in. I knelt, but I didn’t reach for her. I let her decide whether to come close.
She stared at my face, then took one step toward me.
“I’m Aunt Nay,” I said quietly. “I’m here with you.”
She put her hand on my sleeve. I kept my voice gentle. I didn’t ask her what Damian had done. She was three. I wasn’t going to make her answer questions just because my own mind was full of them.
I asked if she wanted to come with me for a little while. She nodded. Then she asked if her mother was there.
I said her mother was safe for now. It wasn’t the whole truth, and I hated that I had to say it that way. But it was the answer I had.

I helped her find her shoes. She held one and kept looking back toward the doorway. I could hear Damian moving around in the other room. My first thought was to rush. My second was that rushing could scare Sofi, or give him a reason to grab her. I had spent years learning what my anger could do. I had not spent years learning how to get a child out of a house.
I took her hand and walked back down the hall.
Damian was standing now. He looked at Sofi, then at me. “Where are you going?”
His mother stood up. His sister set down her phone. Nobody shouted. Somehow that made my hands feel less steady.
Damian stepped between me and the front door. “You’re not taking her anywhere.”
He still thought I was Lidia. I could see that in his face, or I thought I could. I was so focused on getting Sofi out that I didn’t stop to wonder how long the mistake would last.
I kept Sofi behind me. I didn’t touch him. I didn’t threaten him. I said, “Move away from the door.”

His mother said my name, but the name she used was Lidia’s. She told me to stop making a scene. His sister said Sofi needed to stay inside. I could feel that old part of me waking up, the part that used to believe the only way to stop cruelty was to hit harder.
I wanted to hurt him. I did. I wanted him to feel one small piece of what he’d done to Lidia. Then Sofi squeezed my fingers, and I looked down at her hand in mine.

I took Sofi outside through the open doorway and walked fast toward the shop. Damian followed us as far as the front step, calling after me. He didn’t grab me. He didn’t need to. I could hear him behind us, and my legs were shaking by the time we reached the shop.

The woman behind the counter took one look at my face and let us come inside. I asked her to call for emergency help. She did. I sat with Sofi near the counter and kept her hand in mine while I told the person on the phone that a three-year-old had been hit by her father, according to her mother, and that I’d just left the house with her.
I said the next part plainly. “I’m not Lidia. I’m her twin.”

I gave my name. I told them Lidia was still at San Gabriel. I said I had seen bruises on her myself, but the account of what had happened to Sofi came from Lidia. I didn’t want to mix those things up. I’d spent too much of my life being called dangerous because people decided who I was before they heard what happened.

A responder came to speak with me. I told the same story again, including how I’d left the hospital wearing Lidia’s clothes and carrying her ID. It was embarrassing. It could cause trouble for both of us. I told it anyway.

They asked about Sofi’s condition. I told them I hadn’t seen an injury on her that night, and I wouldn’t pretend I had. They spoke with the shopkeeper, then went back toward the house to speak with Damian and the others. I stayed with Sofi. No one announced that the whole matter was settled. They asked questions, wrote down what I said, and made sure Sofi wasn’t sent back into that house that night while they worked out the next steps.

A worker connected to the local support service came to speak with us. She didn’t promise me a quick answer or tell me everything would be fine. She asked where Lidia was and whether I could contact the hospital. I said yes, and this time I made the call.

I explained the switch to the staff at San Gabriel. At first there was a long pause. I could picture the nurse at the door, thinking the woman in Lidia’s clothes was the patient’s twin. I told them Lidia was the woman still there in my gray sweater, and I was Nayeli, the person who had walked out.
“I know this wasn’t okay,” I said. “I’m telling you because you need to know who’s there.”

They checked that Lidia was still at the hospital. They didn’t tell me she could simply leave. They said they needed to speak with her and sort out her identity and care. That was fair. I had made a dangerous mess and could not demand that a nurse fix it in one phone call.

The support worker helped arrange a place where Sofi and I could stay that night while the adults dealt with the immediate questions. I’m not going to dress that up as a rescue. We were safe for those hours. That was enough to be grateful for.

A medical worker checked Sofi. She didn’t tell me what the next decision would be. She wrote down what I had said and what I had seen, and she spoke with Sofi in a calm voice. Sofi mostly wanted to know where her mother was. I said we were working on it.
I went back to San Gabriel with help from the people who were arranging our next steps. I didn’t go in wearing Lidia’s name again. I told the staff who I was before I reached the desk.

Lidia was still in my gray sweater. She looked up when I came in, and her eyes went straight to Sofi. The child ran to her. I stayed where I was for a second. I wanted to scoop them both up and say I’d fixed it. I hadn’t.

The staff spoke with Lidia and checked who she was. They didn’t pretend the mix-up hadn’t happened. I gave them my account of leaving and told them again what I had done. Lidia was offered a chance to speak for herself and ask for care. She took it.
Later, when we had a few minutes alone, Lidia held Sofi close and looked at me.

She didn’t thank me. I didn’t ask her to. I had made the choice for both of us, and even if I’d done it because I was scared for her, it was still my choice. I could love her and still have been wrong about that part.

We talked about the next day. Not the rest of our lives. Just the next day. Lidia wanted to stay where she could get help and speak without Damian or his family standing over her. She wanted Sofi with me while the support worker helped us figure out what could happen next. I agreed, but I told her I wouldn’t make another decision for her without asking.

The worker said she would stay in touch and help us follow up. The reports about Damian and his family still needed to be looked at. Nothing we said in one night could settle every question. But the switch was over. The hospital knew who Lidia was. The people helping us knew who I was. Damian could no longer mistake me for the woman he’d been controlling and call it a private family matter.

Before we left that night, I sat beside Sofi while she leaned against her mother. I noticed my breathing had slowed. At the hospital gate, the air had burned going in. Now I counted each breath without forcing it, one at a time, and kept my hand where Sofi could reach it.
